title: Scheduler priority inversion causing burst serialization — action plan and follow-ups
creator: Maya Chen
description: Summary: During a customer-driven capacity surge test on 2026-02-09 we observed repeated p95/p99 latency spikes and throughput collapse across several pods. Root cause analysis points to a scheduler priority inversion that caused high serialization in the batch assembly path: concurrent high-priority microbursts were preempting slower background batches and causing lock contention in the batch assembler. This contention forced many requests to fall back to serialized handling, which amplified kernel probing frequency and led the path selector to increasingly prefer safe-but-slower kernels. Combined with KV cache cold starts on the same nodes, the net effect was a 3–4x increase in p95 latency and a 30% drop in sustained throughput for ~40 minutes.
timeline: 2026-02-09T09:12: incident alerts triggered. 09:18: ops throttled incoming test traffic to reduce pressure. 09:30: initial rollback of scheduler priority tuning (hotfix v1) rolled to canary. 09:42: global hotfix rollout completed; latency normalized by 09:55. 10:30: post-incident triage and data collection. 2026-02-10: in-depth RCA completed; ownership assigned and follow-ups scheduled.
root_cause: The scheduler's priority queue allowed short-lived high-priority bursts to repeatedly preempt batch assembly workers. The batch assembler uses a coarse lock for pending batches; preemption led to repeated lock acquisitions and forced batch flushes at suboptimal sizes. The flushes increased kernel-probing attempts and evicted some warm KV entries. Path selection code prefers kernels based on recent success rates; the sudden change in observed performance caused it to fall back to conservative kernels until metrics recovered.
impact_details: Affected both hosted and dedicated clusters in us-west-2 under the specific synthetic burst pattern used by customers. Visible symptoms: p95 increased from ~120ms to ~480ms, p99 spikes to >1.2s; throughput dropped ~30% for ~40 minutes. No data loss. A small set of production tenants experienced degraded latency for live traffic routed through the impacted pools (customer-reported errors = low, SLA breaches = none but SLO risk was elevated).
immediate_mitigation_taken: 1) Rate-limited synthetic test traffic and applied a temporary per-tenant burst token to reduce concurrent microbursts. 2) Rolled back scheduler priority thresholds to previous stable values (hotfix v1). 3) Bypassed aggressive kernel probing for the affected canaries (config toggle) while rollback propagated.
long_term_action_items: 1) Replace coarse batch-assembler lock with a sharded lock-free queue (owner: @diego, ENG, estimate 5). 2) Implement priority-aging to prevent starvation and repeated preemption of mid-priority batches (owner: @maya, ENG, estimate 3). 3) Add a quiesce window for kernel probing after a batch reconfiguration to avoid thrashing (owner: @liam, runtime team, estimate 2). 4) KV cache warmup improvements: prefetch strategy for imminent hot keys after a burst (owner: @nisha, estimate 3). 5) Add end-to-end synthetic burst tests to the CI harness and a standalone chaos job that simulates high-frequency microbursts (owner: SRE, estimate 4). 6) Update runbook with clear steps for throttling, toggling kernel-probe flags, and rollback playbook (owner: oncall runbook team). 7) Dashboard and alert changes: new metric 'batcher_lock_hold_time', alert if sustained >200ms and p95 > 2x baseline (owner: observability).
acceptance_criteria: - Sharded queue implemented and bench-tested: p95 under synthetic burst <200ms. - Priority-aging in place and verified with regression tests. - Kernel-probe quiesce window reduces probe rate by >60% during burst in CI tests. - Runbook updated and reviewed by two engineers and SRE. - Dashboards show new metric; alerting validated in staging.
